title: What Is Randomness, Really?
question: Is anything truly random, or is randomness just a word for what we cannot predict?
summary: Randomness splits into ignorance, quantum indeterminacy, and algorithmic incompressibility. These ideas overlap but are not the same, and none gives us a way to certify that something is truly random.
content:
What are we asking?

A coin flip feels random. But a physicist would say that, given the exact force, spin, air currents, and landing surface, the outcome is determined. So is anything truly random, or is randomness merely a name for our ignorance?

Randomness as ignorance

In classical physics, randomness is epistemic. Dice, roulette wheels, and weather are chaotic: tiny differences in starting conditions get amplified until prediction is hopeless in practice. Pseudo-random number generators embody this idea, producing sequences that pass statistical tests while being entirely deterministic from a seed.

Randomness as a property of the world

Quantum mechanics offers a candidate for the real thing. The timing of a single radioactive decay, or which path a photon takes through a beam splitter, appears to have no hidden cause. Bell's theorem and its experimental tests rule out large classes of local hidden-variable explanations, so if you accept standard quantum theory the randomness seems irreducible. Interpretations disagree: pilot-wave theory restores determinism at the price of nonlocality, and many-worlds says every outcome happens, so randomness is an artifact of a branch's perspective.

Can you define it mathematically?

Surprisingly, yes. Kolmogorov complexity defines a string as random if no program significantly shorter than the string can reproduce it. A random sequence is incompressible: it has no pattern to exploit. The sting is that complexity is uncomputable, so we can never be certain a given sequence is random. We can only prove the opposite by finding a short description.

Humans are also bad intuitive judges. We think streaks of heads are "non-random" when real randomness produces them routinely, and when asked to fake random sequences we alternate too much.

Why it matters

Cryptography depends on unpredictable keys; weak randomness has broken real systems. Monte Carlo methods use randomness to solve problems that deterministic methods cannot touch. Evolution leans on mutation. And randomness plays a role in debates about free will: if our choices follow chaotic physics, or quantum noise, does either rescue agency?

perspectives.title: Classical physics
perspectives.description: Randomness is practical unpredictability from chaos and incomplete information, not a feature of nature.

perspectives.title: Quantum mechanics
perspectives.description: Individual measurement outcomes appear to lack any hidden cause, making randomness fundamental, unless an interpretation like pilot-wave theory says otherwise.

perspectives.title: Algorithmic information theory
perspectives.description: A sequence is random if it is incompressible, though this can never be verified for a particular string.

perspectives.title: Cryptography and computing
perspectives.description: Randomness is a resource: its quality determines the security of keys and the reliability of simulations.

connections: Cognitive biases about streaks and the gambler's fallacy
openQuestions: Is quantum randomness truly irreducible or a feature of our interpretation?
Could a deterministic universe still contain real randomness in any meaningful sense?
How can we ever certify that a physical source is truly random?
Does the distinction between ignorance and fundamental chance matter for how we should live?
